messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 48
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 47

The memory of the attic door clicking shut does not leave him. It anchors him to eight years ago, to the afternoon when he was forty, working a residential repair job in a quiet suburb. The homeowner’s brother steps into the crawlspace to hand him a tool, then pins him against the wooden beams. No one calls for help. The house stays still. When he finally slips out, the fiberglass insulation clings to his work pants like ash. He is forty-eight now. His hands are mapped with calluses and old burns, his shoulders broad from years of hauling shingles and navigating steep pitches. In his Oceania family, men traditionally carry silence like a tool, and he learned early to work through the discomfort, to keep the head down and the hands busy. He still shows up to job sites at dawn, boots laced tight, coffee thermos in hand. But the roof, once a place of steady rhythm, now feels like a grid of potential exits. He checks doorways first. He sits with his back to the wall. When a client leans over his shoulder to inspect flashing, his breath catches. He tells himself it is just the heat, the exertion, the dust. He does not say that his pulse drums in his throat like a trapped bird. At home, the distance between him and his wife has grown into something quiet and heavy. They share a bed, but he sleeps with one eye open, listening for the floorboards. When she touches his arm, he flinches before he remembers who she is. He wants to tell her, to name the weight, but the words catch somewhere behind his ribs. He worries that if he speaks it, it will become real in a way he cannot unmake. So he works longer hours. He fixes gutters on rainy Sundays. He tells himself he is just being careful. Memories come without warning. The smell of wet shingles in July brings back the taste of metal and dust. A dropped wrench sounds like a lock turning. He wakes at 3 a.m., heart racing, staring at the ceiling fan until his breathing slows. During the day, he moves through conversations like a man wading through waist-deep water. His wife asks about his week. He says the usual. He laughs when she jokes about the weather. Inside, the ground feels thin. The trauma screen he filled out last month tallied a number that sits heavier than any bag of shingles. Forty-seven. The clinical language feels distant, but the score echoes in the way he holds himself at the job site. He goes to therapy now, every Thursday at four. He sits in the same chair, the one with the worn arms. He talks about the roof. He talks about the insulation, the angle of the trusses, the way sunlight cuts through a half-open window. He does not yet talk about the hands that held him down. But he notices things he used to ignore. He notices how his jaw stays clenched during client meetings. He notices how he scans every room he enters. He notices that he no longer feels the sun on his neck without looking for an exit. Yesterday, he measures a new roof pitch while the wind pushes against his shoulders. He stands at the ridge, tape measure in hand, and feels the familiar tightness behind his eyes. He breathes out. He marks the timber. He climbs down the ladder slowly, step by step, until his boots find the grass. He walks to his truck, opens the door, and sits for a long moment before starting the engine. The radio plays a quiet song. He turns it off. He puts the key in the ignition anyway.
